Transistors and the Front End

Only TSMC, Intel and Samsung make 2 nm-class transistors in volume. TSMC plans its A14 process for 2028, with more than 20 percent higher logic density than N2.

Transistors and the Front End, stage 8 of 15Next stage: 09 Foundries and Fabs

ConcentrationExtremeHigh

In plain terms

The front end of a chip factory is the part that builds the transistors, the billions of tiny switches in every chip. Each switch works like a valve. Current runs along a narrow strip of silicon called the channel, and a small voltage on a gate above the strip opens or shuts the flow. For decades chipmakers made the strips shorter, so they switched faster and more of them fit on a chip. But once the strip gets short enough, the valve stops sealing. Current leaks through even when the gate is off, and the chip burns power doing nothing. The newest kind of transistor, called gate-all-around, cuts this leak by wrapping the gate around all four sides of the strip. Building them takes a long sequence of steps that have to run in exact order. Only three companies, TSMC, Intel and Samsung, make these switches in volume. In 2024 the United States put a worldwide license requirement on the know-how for building them, with an exception for countries that impose matching controls.

In short

Intel's 18A process shipped gate-all-around transistors together with backside power, a second power network built underneath them[11]. TSMC says its A14 process will give up to 15 percent more speed or up to 30 percent less power than N2[31]. Rapidus, a state-backed newcomer in Japan, said in July 2025 that it would begin 2 nm mass production in 2027[20].

China's SMIC makes 7 nm-class chips without extreme-ultraviolet (EUV) lithography, one way of printing chip patterns[19]. China has announced $43 billion to develop its own EUV[30]. In September 2025 the Center for Strategic and International Studies judged that EUV remains firmly out of reach[30].

Why substitution is slow
A newcomer has to work out its own process flow, which sets the steps, their order and the tools for each. Rapidus is building its flow on IBM's 2 nm technology. Three firms run a gate-all-around flow in volume. China cannot buy extreme-ultraviolet scanners.
Where China stands

SMIC ships a process it calls N+3, measured at 113.4 million transistors per square millimeter. It prints its tightest layers in several passes because it cannot buy an extreme-ultraviolet scanner.

Where the US stands

Intel runs the only American-owned line that makes the newest transistors. Its 18A process brought gate-all-around transistors and backside power to market together.

Specimen · gate-all-around transistor

A gate-all-around transistor, the switch in a 2 nm-class chip, drawn at true proportions. The three silicon sheets are each 6 nm thick and 30 nm wide: a few dozen atoms from top to bottom, and roughly ten thousand times thinner than a human hair. The gold cage is the gate metal wrapping all four sides of each sheet.

See it in 3D in the interactive chapter

Nvidia's Blackwell GPU holds 208 billion switches on two dies, each die the largest a lithography machine can print in one shot[1]. Every switch has to turn on fully, let almost no current through when off, and keep doing it for years. Making the switches is called the front end of line. Wiring them together is the back end of line.

How it works

The front end builds the transistors in a fixed order, starting with the channel. In a FinFET, the older design, the fab etches the silicon into thin fins that stand up from the wafer. The gate then goes over the top and both sides of each fin, three sides instead of one.

In a gate-all-around transistor, the fab instead grows alternating layers of silicon and silicon-germanium and cuts the stack into narrow bars[2]. It lays a placeholder, called a dummy gate, across each bar where the real gate will go[3]. On either side of the placeholder it cuts deep trenches where the source and drain, the two ends of the channel, will go[4]. Through those trenches it etches the silicon-germanium layers back a little and fills the gaps with an insulator, the inner spacer, which keeps the gate apart from the source and drain[2]. Then it grows the source and drain as crystal inside the trenches, a step called epitaxy[4].

Only then does the fab remove the placeholder and dissolve the silicon-germanium, leaving thin silicon sheets that hang between the source and drain like shelves[2]. The inner spacer shields the source and drain from that etch[3]. The fab coats every sheet with an insulating film a few atoms thick, so the gate can control the channel without touching it. Gate metal then fills the gaps above, below and beside each sheet, covering all four sides[5]. Last come the contacts, small metal plugs down to the source, the drain and the gate, ready for the wiring layers above.

Each of those steps is a separate deposition, etch or implant. An implant step, called ion implantation, fires atoms of boron or phosphorus into chosen patches of silicon so they conduct the way the design needs. The steps have to run in exact order, because later layers cover earlier ones. Once gate metal surrounds a sheet, the insulator can no longer go between them.

Current leaks two ways, straight through the gate insulator and along the channel from end to end while the gate is off. The second is called short-channel leakage, and wrapping the gate around the channel reduces it. Three fixes deal with the two leaks:

  • Better insulator. A thicker hafnium-based film, paired with a metal gate, lets fewer electrons slip straight through yet controls the channel as tightly as before. Intel replaced the silicon dioxide insulator with it at 45 nm in 2007[6]. It said the new film cut leakage through the insulator more than tenfold and, with the metal gate, leakage along the channel more than fivefold[6].
  • More gate. Fins and nanosheets wrap gate metal around more sides of the channel.
  • Thinner channel. The fab thins the silicon until no current can flow where the gate cannot reach it.

Variants and trade-offs

Planar and FinFET

A planar transistor lays the gate on one side of a flat channel. As the channel shortens, the gate loses control of it. A fin stands the channel on edge so the gate covers three sides. But each fin adds a fixed amount of current, so a designer who needs more current has to add a whole fin.

Gate-all-around nanosheets

A nanosheet transistor lays the channel flat again, stacks two to four thin sheets and wraps gate metal around each one. The sheets can be drawn at different widths, so current can be set in finer steps. TSMC sells this as NanoFlex, which lets designers mix short logic cells for small area with tall cells for performance[7].

TSMC's N2, its first nanosheet node, entered volume production in the fourth quarter of 2025[8]. TSMC rates the follow-on N2P at 18 percent more speed at the same power and 36 percent less power at the same speed than its earlier N3E[9]. It gives N2P 1.2 times the logic density of N3E and 1.15 times its chip density, two separate measures[9].

Intel's version, called RibbonFET, is built into its 18A process, which Intel says is in high-volume production in the United States[10]. An improved version, 18A-P, adds another 9 percent performance at the same power[11]. Samsung began initial production of its 3 nm gate-all-around process in June 2022, more than three years before TSMC's N2[12]. But SemiAnalysis reported in February 2023 that, because of yield problems, high-volume chips on Samsung's 3 nm gate-all-around technology were expected only in 2024[13].

Those numbers are the foundries' own claims until someone measures the silicon. Each foundry picks its own baseline, and none publishes a density figure that can be compared with a rival's.

Backside power delivery

In a conventional chip, power and signal share one stack of copper wiring above the transistors, where wide power rails crowd out the signal wires. With backside power, the fab grinds the wafer thin and builds a second network for power underneath it.

Intel's version, PowerVia, is part of 18A, and Intel calls it an industry first[10]. It cut routed area by 11 percent and dynamic voltage droop tenfold[11]. Droop is the sag in supply voltage when a block of logic switches on at once. TSMC's Super Power Rail connects the backside network directly to each transistor's source and drain, the two ends of its channel. Against N2P, TSMC rates A16, which uses Super Power Rail, at 8 to 10 percent more speed, 15 to 20 percent less power and up to 1.10 times the chip density[9].

TSMC said in April 2026 that two more processes, A13 and A12, are scheduled to enter production in 2029[14]. A13 is a direct shrink of A14 with 6 percent area savings, and A12 adds Super Power Rail to the A14 platform[14].

CFET and what comes after

A basic logic circuit needs two transistors that switch on opposite signals, and in production chips the two sit side by side. Complementary field-effect transistors, or CFETs, stack the two on top of each other[15]. The research institute imec sees them as an attractive design for logic nodes beyond 1 nm[15].

The back end of line

Wiring has become as hard to make as the transistor. Copper seeps into the insulator around it, so every wire needs a barrier, a liner and a cap[16]. As the most critical wiring levels drop below a 20 nm pitch, those extra layers take a large share of the wire's width[16]. Pitch is the distance from the center of one wire to the center of the next. Two metals are moving into those narrow levels.

  • Ruthenium shows promise for use without a barrier, which would keep the wire's resistance low[16]. imec has demonstrated ruthenium lines at a 16 nm pitch[17].
  • Molybdenum conducts worse than copper in bulk, with a resistivity of 5.3 microhm-cm against copper's 1.68[18]. But in a thin film it beats tungsten by up to 30 percent and needs no barrier either, so chipmakers are putting it into some contacts and local wiring layers[18].

Who makes it

TSMC, Intel and Samsung build gate-all-around nodes with extreme-ultraviolet (EUV) lithography. China's SMIC builds 7 nm-class nodes without it[19].

In July 2025 Rapidus, a state-backed newcomer in Japan, said it had started making 2 nm prototypes at its plant in Chitose, Hokkaido, and would begin mass production in 2027[20]. Its process builds on IBM's 2 nm technology, which the two firms agreed in December 2022 to develop further for production at Rapidus's plant in Japan[21]. By June 2026 Rapidus had raised 424.95 billion yen in equity, the latest 150 billion yen from a state agency[22]. It has also received government research subsidies since fiscal 2022[22].

A node's name, such as 7 nm, does not measure any feature on the chip. Applied Materials, a toolmaker, said in 2022 that chipmakers raise density in two ways, by printing smaller features and by laying out each logic cell more tightly[5]. SMIC's N+3, its third-generation 7 nm process, sets its narrowest wires 32.5 nm apart, tighter than Intel 18A's 36 nm, though SemiAnalysis called that comparison an incomplete, cherry-picked metric[19]. It packs 113.4 million transistors per square millimeter, against 107.7 for TSMC's N6[19].

AI accelerators have usually trailed the leading edge. A die as large as theirs is more likely to hold a defect[23]. So the share of dies that work, called the yield, gets high enough only once a process has run long enough to cut its defect rate.

Blackwell uses a custom TSMC 4NP process[1]. AMD's MI455X, launched on 23 July 2026, lists TSMC 2 nm and 3 nm silicon[24]. It spreads its compute across eight separate dies[25].

SRAM, the fast memory on the logic die, is the part whose failure to shrink hurts AI chips most. TSMC claims 22 percent more SRAM density from N3E to N2[26]. But the gain comes mostly from the circuits around the memory array, and the cell that holds one bit shrinks little or not at all[26]. See Memory and HBM.

The chokepoint

TSMC, Intel and Samsung do not sell their process flows, which set the steps, their order and the tools for each. In September 2024 the United States put a worldwide license requirement on the know-how for building gate-all-around transistors, with an exception for countries that impose matching controls[27].

China launched its third National Integrated Circuit Fund in May 2024 with 344 billion yuan, about $47 billion[28]. But China cannot buy EUV scanners.

A Shanghai state firm began building domestic immersion scanners in 2026 and planned about five that year and roughly 20 in 2027[29]. Those are deep-ultraviolet machines, a generation behind EUV. SMIC gets fine features out of them by printing its tightest layers in several passes[19]. That many scanners keep those lines running but come nowhere near replacing ASML, the Dutch scanner maker.

Domestic EUV is further off. China has announced $43 billion to develop it[30]. In September 2025 the Center for Strategic and International Studies (CSIS) judged that EUV remains firmly out of reach despite massive state investment[30].

See Lithography and Geopolitics.

Review questions

Open a question to see its answer.

Why do the newest transistors wrap the gate around the channel?

To cut the current that leaks when the switch is off.

The gate turns the current along the channel on and off. Shorter channels switch faster but leak more. A gate on all four sides cuts that leakage further than a fin, whose gate covers three sides. Reread: How it works

Which companies make these gate-all-around transistors in volume?

TSMC, Intel and Samsung.

Samsung began initial 3 nm production with them in June 2022. TSMC's N2 process entered volume production in the fourth quarter of 2025, and Intel's 18A process is in high-volume manufacturing. Reread: Who makes it

Why is the front end, the part of a fab that builds the transistors, hard for a new firm to enter?

TSMC, Intel and Samsung do not sell their leading-edge process flows, the exact sequence of steps that builds the transistors.

A newcomer has to develop its own flow or build on another firm's technology, as Rapidus is doing with IBM's 2 nm process. Reread: The chokepoint

How does China's SMIC make advanced chips without an EUV machine?

It builds its tightest layers in several patterning steps on deep-ultraviolet tools.

Export controls block ASML from selling SMIC an EUV machine. With this method SMIC makes chips on N+3, its third-generation 7 nm process. Reread: The chokepoint
